planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; established plants tolerate short dry spells better than most soft shield fern forms.

directions: This heirloom soft shield fern selection produces unusually broad, densely overlapping pinnae with jagged, congested edges that give the whole frond a bold, ruffled texture distinct from the lacier straight species. Plant divisions in rich, humus-heavy soil in partial to full shade and mulch to keep roots cool through summer heat. Fronds are evergreen to semi-evergreen in milder zones, providing structure through winter when many companion perennials have died back. Groom out tattered old fronds in late winter just before the new croziers unfurl.

planting.note: Plant divisions in rich, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this refined selection resents both waterlogging and prolonged drought.

directions: Discovered in England in the 1870s and still regarded as one of the finest soft shield fern selections ever found, this cultivar carries exceptionally finely divided, plumose fronds that arch gracefully into a soft, feathery mound unlike any other Polystichum form. Plant divisions into humus-rich soil in a sheltered, shaded site and keep evenly moist while the crown establishes. Its dissected texture makes it a striking specimen fern for a shaded rock garden or woodland border where its lacy detail can be appreciated up close. Remove old fronds in late winter before new growth emerges.

planting.note: Plant divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; its compact size suits a shaded trough or the front of a woodland border.

directions: A dwarf, tightly congested form of soft shield fern with short, densely crowded pinnae that give each frond a compact, almost ruffled outline rather than the loose, arching habit of the species. Its diminutive scale makes it well suited to shaded rock gardens, fern troughs, or the front edge of a woodland bed where full-size Polystichum cultivars would overwhelm. Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade and divide congested crowns only occasionally, as growth is naturally slow. Remove any winter-damaged fronds in early spring before new croziers appear.

planting.note: Plant divisions in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; this heirloom crested form performs best where lady fern is already well adapted.

directions: A Victorian-era selection of lady fern prized for its heavily crested, congested frond tips and secondary crests along each pinna, giving mature clumps a dense, tasseled silhouette quite unlike the airy, finely cut straight species. Plant divisions in evenly moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade and keep the crown from drying out during its first season. Best sited where its unusual crested texture can be viewed up close, such as along a shaded path edge or in a collector's fern bed. Cut back the deciduous fronds to the crown after they die down in fall.

planting.note: Plant divisions in evenly moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring, watering deeply until new fronds are fully expanded.

directions: One of the many named fronds-forms collected during the Victorian fern-craze, this lady fern selection produces gracefully tasseled, multi-crested pinnae along an otherwise typical arching frond, creating a softer and lacier crested effect than the bolder Grandiceps types. Grow in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade alongside hostas and other woodland perennials, where its unusual texture provides quiet novelty rather than a bold accent. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain vigor and propagate true divisions of the crest.

planting.note: Plant divisions in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; small scale suits a fern trough or the front of a shaded rock garden.

directions: A miniature form of the common lady fern that reproduces the species' finely cut, lacy frond texture at a fraction of the scale, forming a tidy tuft rarely more than ten inches tall. Its diminutive habit makes it a natural choice for shaded rock gardens, fern troughs, and the front edge of a woodland border where a full-size lady fern would quickly dominate. Plant in humus-rich, consistently moist soil in partial to full shade and avoid crowding by larger neighbors that could shade it out entirely. Cut the deciduous fronds back to the crown once they collapse after the first hard frost.
